entries.1:1: A famine hit Israel during the time of the judges, so a man from Bethlehem took his wife and two sons to live in Moab to survive. Hard times can push ordinary families to make difficult moves.
entries.1:2: The man was Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their sons Mahlon and Chilion, and they settled in Moab for a while. This introduces the family whose story the book will follow.
entries.1:3: Elimelech died, leaving Naomi alone with her two sons. A family's plans can be shattered by loss, and Naomi's hardship is only beginning.
entries.1:4: The sons married Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth, and the family stayed there about ten years. These marriages set up the loyalty and love that will matter later in the story.
entries.1:5: Both sons also died, so Naomi was left with no husband and no sons. She lost nearly everything that gave her security, and her grief is real.
entries.1:6: Naomi heard that God had blessed his people with food again, so she prepared to return home with her daughters-in-law. News of hope gave her a reason to go back.
entries.1:7: Naomi left the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law went with her toward Judah. The journey home begins with all three women together.
entries.1:8: Naomi urged her daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' homes and asked God to bless them for their kindness to her and to the dead. She put their welfare ahead of her own need for company.
entries.1:9: Naomi prayed that God would give each of them rest and security in a new marriage, then kissed them, and they all wept loudly. Saying goodbye to people you love is deeply painful.
entries.1:10: Both women insisted they would go back with Naomi to her people. Their love for her made them willing to leave their own homeland.
entries.1:11: Naomi told them to go back and asked whether she could possibly have more sons who could become their husbands. She was pointing out honestly that she had nothing left to offer them.
entries.1:12: Naomi said she was too old to marry again, and even if she remarried and had sons that very night, it would not help. She was being realistic about her age and situation.
entries.1:13: Naomi asked whether the women would wait for sons who might be born, which would be absurd, and said she was sadder for them than for herself because God's hand had gone against her. She felt her suffering was also hurting those who loved her.
entries.1:14: They wept again, and Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, but Ruth refused to leave her. The two women made different choices, and Ruth's choice shows deep loyalty.
entries.1:15: Naomi told Ruth that Orpah had gone back to her people and her gods, and urged Ruth to follow her. She was giving Ruth a free way out.
entries.1:16: Ruth begged Naomi not to make her leave, promising to go where Naomi goes, stay where she stays, and adopt Naomi's people and God as her own. This is a powerful promise of loyalty that puts relationship above comfort.
entries.1:17: Ruth vowed that she would die and be buried where Naomi dies, and called on the Lord to punish her if anything but death separated them. She made an unbreakable commitment.
entries.1:18: When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped arguing. Sometimes the right response to someone's firm love is to accept it.
entries.1:19: The two women traveled to Bethlehem, and the whole town was stirred up about them, asking if this was really Naomi. Her return drew attention because people remembered her.
entries.1:20: Naomi told them not to call her Naomi but Mara, meaning bitter, because God had made her life very hard. She was honest about her pain instead of pretending everything was fine.
entries.1:21: Naomi said she left with plenty and came back empty, and asked why they would still call her Naomi when the Lord had brought sorrow on her. She felt God had turned against her, and she said so plainly.
entries.1:22: Naomi returned from Moab with Ruth, and they arrived in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. The timing matters because the harvest will provide food and a way forward for these two poor women.
entries.2:1: Naomi had a wealthy relative on her husband's side named Boaz. This matters because he will become the key person who helps the two women survive.
entries.2:2: Ruth asks Naomi for permission to go into the fields and pick up leftover grain behind the workers. This was a humble way for a poor person to get food, and Ruth is willing to do it.
entries.2:3: Ruth went out and happened to end up in a field owned by Boaz, a relative of her father-in-law. What looked like chance was really the start of God's help for them.
entries.2:4: Boaz arrived and greeted his workers with a blessing, and they blessed him back. This shows he was a kind and respectful boss.
entries.2:5: Boaz noticed Ruth and asked his foreman who she was. He was paying attention to a stranger in his field.
entries.2:6: The foreman told him she was the Moabite woman who had come back from Moab with Naomi. Everyone knew her story.
entries.2:7: The foreman said Ruth had politely asked to gather grain and had worked hard all morning without a break. She was humble and diligent.
entries.2:8: Boaz tells Ruth to stay in his field and keep close to his young women workers. He is offering her safety and protection.
entries.2:9: Boaz tells her to follow the women cutting grain, promises the men won't bother her, and says she can drink from the water his workers have. He is looking out for her needs.
entries.2:10: Ruth bows down and asks why Boaz would notice her, since she is a foreigner. She is surprised by his kindness.
entries.2:11: Boaz says he has heard how Ruth left her own parents and homeland to stay with Naomi after her husband died. He respects her loyalty and sacrifice.
entries.2:12: Boaz asks God to reward Ruth and says she has come under God's protection. He is praying that God will bless her for what she has done.
entries.2:13: Ruth thanks Boaz and says his kind words have comforted her, even though she isn't one of his own servants. She feels encouraged and valued.
entries.2:14: At mealtime Boaz invites Ruth to eat with his workers and even gives her extra roasted grain. She eats until she is full, showing his generosity.
entries.2:15: When Ruth went back to work, Boaz told his men to let her gather grain even among the bundles and not to embarrass her. He quietly made her work easier.
entries.2:16: Boaz also told the men to pull out some grain and leave it for her, and to speak kindly to her. He went out of his way to provide for her.
entries.2:17: Ruth gathered grain until evening, then threshed it, and it came to about a full ephah, a large amount. Her hard work paid off with enough food for many days.
entries.2:18: Ruth carried the grain home, showed Naomi what she had gathered, and gave her the food she had left over. She shared generously with her mother-in-law.
entries.2:19: Naomi asked where Ruth had worked and asked God to bless the man who helped her. When Ruth said it was Boaz, Naomi recognized his name.
entries.2:20: Naomi praised God for his kindness and told Ruth that Boaz is a close relative, one of their family guardians. This was very good news for their future.
entries.2:21: Ruth told Naomi that Boaz had invited her to stay close to his workers until the whole harvest was finished. That meant steady food and safety for weeks.
entries.2:22: Naomi agreed it was safer for Ruth to stay with Boaz's servant girls than to go to another field where she might be harmed. She was protecting her daughter-in-law.
entries.2:23: Ruth stayed with Boaz's workers through the barley and wheat harvests and kept living with Naomi. She worked steadily and remained loyal to her mother-in-law.
entries.3:1: Naomi wants to find a safe, secure home for Ruth, her widowed daughter-in-law. It shows that love in a family means actively looking out for the other person's future and security.
entries.3:2: Naomi points out that Boaz, a relative who could protect them, is working at the threshing floor that night. She is making a careful plan based on what she knows about him and the situation.
entries.3:3: Naomi tells Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, then go to Boaz but stay out of sight until he has finished eating. This was a practical way to prepare for a serious, respectful approach to him.
entries.3:4: Naomi tells Ruth to notice where Boaz lies down, then uncover his feet and lie there, and he will tell her what to do. Ruth is being asked to trust her mother-in-law's guidance and to let Boaz take the lead.
entries.3:5: Ruth simply agrees to do everything Naomi has told her. Her answer shows her trust in Naomi and her willingness to follow a plan that could change her whole life.
entries.3:6: Ruth goes to the threshing floor and carries out Naomi's instructions exactly. Her obedience shows she is serious about seeking a secure future and is willing to act on good advice.
entries.3:7: After Boaz has eaten and drunk and is in good spirits, he lies down by the grain, and Ruth quietly comes and lies at his feet. She is following the plan carefully and discreetly.
entries.3:8: In the middle of the night Boaz wakes with a start and is startled to find a woman lying at his feet. The scene shows how unexpected and bold Ruth's action was.
entries.3:9: Boaz asks who she is, and Ruth identifies herself and asks him to take her as his wife because he is a close relative. She is openly asking him to accept the responsibility of protecting and providing for her.
entries.3:10: Boaz blesses Ruth and praises her for choosing to seek a family protector rather than chasing after younger men, rich or poor. He recognizes her loyalty and good character.
entries.3:11: Boaz tells Ruth not to be afraid and promises to do whatever she asks, because everyone in town knows she is a woman of good character. He reassures her that her reputation and request are respected.
entries.3:12: Boaz admits he is a close relative, but there is an even closer one who has the first right to act. He is being honest and fair rather than rushing to take what was not yet his to take.
entries.3:13: Boaz tells Ruth to stay the night, and in the morning he will let the closer relative do his duty if he will; if not, Boaz swears before God that he himself will marry her. He promises to settle the matter properly and without delay.
entries.3:14: Ruth stays at his feet until morning and leaves before it is light enough for people to recognize each other, and Boaz asks that her visit be kept quiet. He is protecting her reputation while the matter is still unresolved.
entries.3:15: Boaz tells Ruth to hold out her cloak, and he pours six measures of grain into it for her to carry back to town. This is a generous gift that shows his care for her and for Naomi.
entries.3:16: When Ruth gets home, Naomi asks how things went, and Ruth tells her everything Boaz had done. The two women share the outcome openly and honestly.
entries.3:17: Ruth explains that Boaz gave her the grain so she would not return to Naomi empty-handed. The gift is a sign of his kindness and a pledge that he is taking the situation seriously.
entries.3:18: Naomi tells Ruth to wait quietly and see what happens, because Boaz will not rest until he has settled the matter that day. She is confident that Boaz will keep his word and act quickly.
entries.4:1: Boaz went to the town gate, where business was done, and called over the closer relative and some witnesses. He wanted to settle the family matter publicly and fairly.
entries.4:2: Boaz gathered ten town leaders to sit as official witnesses. This made the agreement legal and public, so no one could dispute it later.
entries.4:3: Boaz told the closer relative that Naomi was selling the family land that had belonged to Elimelech. He was explaining the deal before offering it to him.
entries.4:4: Boaz offered the relative the first chance to buy the land, as the law required, and the man agreed to do it. Boaz was being fair by letting the closer relative decide first.
entries.4:5: Boaz added that whoever bought the land also had to marry Ruth and keep her dead husband's family name alive. The deal came with a responsibility, not just property.
entries.4:6: The closer relative backed out because taking on Ruth and the land could harm his own family's inheritance. He gave up his right to Boaz.
entries.4:7: In those days, a man took off his sandal and gave it to the other person to seal a deal. It was the public way of making an agreement official.
entries.4:8: The closer relative told Boaz to take the land and handed over his sandal as proof. He was officially giving up his claim.
entries.4:9: Boaz announced to the witnesses that he had legally bought all the property that had belonged to Elimelech and his sons. He made the purchase public and official.
entries.4:10: Boaz also announced that he was marrying Ruth to keep her dead husband's name and memory alive. The witnesses were there to confirm both the land deal and the marriage.
entries.4:11: The people and leaders agreed to be witnesses and blessed the couple. They prayed that Ruth would be like Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel, and that Boaz would prosper.
entries.4:12: They prayed that Boaz's family would be as great as Perez's family, which came from Tamar and Judah. They were asking God to bless the children Boaz and Ruth would have.
entries.4:13: Boaz married Ruth, and God gave her a son. This was the happy result of her loyalty and Boaz's kindness.
entries.4:14: The women praised God for giving Naomi a grandson and a family line to carry on. They saw this as God's kindness to her after her loss.
entries.4:15: They told Naomi the child would bring her new life and care for her in old age. They praised Ruth, whose love for Naomi was worth more than seven sons.
entries.4:16: Naomi took the baby and held him close, caring for him as her own. Her emptiness and grief were replaced with joy and purpose.
entries.4:17: The neighbor women named the baby Obed, which means servant or worshiper, and he became the grandfather of King David. This ordinary family became part of God's plan for Israel's greatest king.
entries.4:18: The book ends with a family list starting with Perez. This shows the family line that led from the past to the present.
entries.4:19: The list continues through Hezron, Ram, and Amminadab. Each name shows the family line moving forward through the generations.
entries.4:20: The family line goes on through Nahshon and Salmon. These names connect the earlier generations to Boaz.
entries.4:21: Salmon was Boaz's father, and Boaz was Obed's father. This ties Boaz and Ruth directly into the family line.
entries.4:22: Obed was Jesse's father, and Jesse was David's father. The story ends by showing that Ruth, a foreigner, became the great-grandmother of King David.
